description_full: Omnicell, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides healthcare technology in the United States and internationally. It offers hospital and health systems solutions, such as points of care for clinician workflows in patient care areas of the healthcare system; Titan XT, an automated dispensing system; XTExtend, a console swap for its XT cabinets; and Central Pharmacy Dispensing Service for the medication dispensing process. The company also provides Central Med Automation Service for medication dispensing; IV Compounding Service, an in-house compounding system; specialty pharmacy services, including turnkey solution to help health systems establish, manage, and optimize an entity-owned specialty pharmacy; EnlivenHealth platform to digitally enable retail and community pharmacies; medication adherence solutions comprising consumables and medication packaging systems; and technology implementation, customer education and training, program management, and related offerings to professional services. In addition, it offers post-installation support and maintenance via phone and/or web, on-site service, parts, and access to software upgrades; software and hardware products for full traceability of medicines and medical supplies throughout the healthcare system; OmniSphere, a cloud-based platform. The company was formerly known as Omnicell Technologies, Inc. and changed its name to Omnicell, Inc. in 2001. Omnicell, Inc. was incorporated in 1992 and is headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas.

financial_summary: Omnicell, Inc. is a small-cap healthcare business with a $1.5B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 0% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 47%.

The business throws off $87M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 62.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
